Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

The end times for new entrants into math research is really here now isn’t it , who will even need a post-doc !

Projecting that further into future: After post-docs become mostly redundant, grad students will be next. After that, the profs. Those that remain, if any, are the best of the very best.

Kevin Cheung said:

Projecting that further into future: After post-docs become mostly redundant, grad students will be next. After that, the profs. Those that remain, if any, are the best of the very best.

The reports of the death of human mathematicians are exaggerations! No human in the mathematics community will be made redundant, since AI tools are just that – tools – and cannot take responsibility for their output

By that logic, how do you explain e.g. many humans working on software engineering -- including "sensitive" systems like payment processing, security, etc -- that have been made redundant and laid off?

First of all mathematics is a human activity. It is humans who decide what is mathematically interesting based on what we can state and prove. So AI replacing mathematics in any meaningful sense is fantasy. AI will always play catch up with humans since we define what is and isn't good mathematics.

What we see happening is people who control AI having the power to decide where society's resources are allocated through financial means and control of firms and AI hypers breathlessly promoting this nonsense. So there is risk of loss of funding.

Jeremy Tan said:

The reports of the death of human mathematicians are exaggerations! No human in the mathematics community will be made redundant, since AI tools are just that – tools – and cannot take responsibility for their output

The realistic fear isn't that mathematicians are suddenly going to be fired overnight. The realistic fear is that AI automation of mathematics (real or perceived) is going to precipitate a shift in funding priorities that could starve mathematics as an academic institution.

AI companies are going around insinuating that they're going to 'solve' mathematics:

’Eventually AI will solve all mathematics.’ one of the Deep Mind members said

image.png

And I've heard some people in the industry are going so far as to say that mathematics is already a 'solved problem'.

How much of a leap is it for politicians to say "why do we need to fund human mathematicians if computers are just going to be able to do that stuff anyway?"?

In the US, obviously there are other factors at play but we have already seen a pretty big shift in funding priority which was to some extent made in the name of pivoting to AI research. Because of this general shift, admissions to graduate schools have been down for the last two years. (I'm also hearing that the post-doc market is similarly rough.)

Given this I think it's pretty naive to insist that there's no reason to be worried about the possibility of AI having a deleterious effect on mathematics as an institution.

which suggests that it is time we consider who owns and controls AI and how we allocate society's resources. There is no reason to continue allowing OpenAI or Anthropic or anybody else to own their models. These models are built on the labour of underpaid workers, and data of humans taken without their consent.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

which suggests that it is time we consider who owns and controls AI and how we allocate society's resources.

They've already done this in Europe with the Artificial Intelligence Act
7 messages were moved here from #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Don Knuth and Claude by Joachim Breitner.
Just my personal opinion: I would suggest changing the title of this thread!

I have just used an LLM (not going to specify which one) to look an exam for one of my courses. It answered every question perfectly. What's more, it identified an error in one of the questions and corrected it.

@Jeremy Tan if you are describing this act : https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/
I am not sure how it addressed ownership
How do you teach the average students these days when they know that AI has far surpassed their abilities?
You teach them how to use it. They have to decide what is worthwhile mathematics later in their careers. Not AI.
Also the title of this thread is a bit alarmist and extreme (using the word "death"). Let's please tone it down or make it less personal
The title wasn't set by me. I don't know who set it.
I changed the title
If we ever get to a point where we outsource all mathematics to AI, mathematics devolves into chaos or stagnates, depending on the incentive structure of the AI.

Mathematics is a human creation for humans to comprehend patterns. If you gave AI all the data Kepler had as training data, it would probably produce a billion parameter model that could predict every planet's position. It would also be spectacularly useless as a model for us humans to igorously understand and iterate upon.

Let's do a though experiment. Say you are teaching linear algebra. AI can do everything in the course perfectly and explain things better than 99% of all the instructors out there. What do you assess students on?
On what they understand
Oral exams
with whiteboards. Like they do in Denmark
Our classes here for linear algebra are over 150 students.
Well, let's have AI do the exams at scale then, guided by human instructors.
I think as somone still doing coursework, you underestimate how much of modern math is built out of humans struggling with proofs, finding new abstractions, proofs, and definitions and so on.
I used to do that too.
Basically, you are saying that students will mostly learn from AI and be assessed by AI.
No
I am saying humans will still have to learn and comprehend and build on what they learn, and demonstrate it.

James E Hanson said:

Given this I think it's pretty naive to insist that there's no reason to be worried about the possibility of AI having a deleterious effect on mathematics as an institution.

There are real reasons to be worried, as many people (including me) have raised in this channel's threads. But it is also counterproductive to talk about fears and worst-case scenarios instead of the measures that can be taken to alleviate the worries.

The overarching theme of the measures taken so far seems to be something I've said before: AI systems are tools, not gods. You have to cite them as if you had used Mathematica, mpmath, SymPy or any other non-AI software. You have to show that you understand the AI output yourself. And so on.
Agreed. Also this discussion is becoming off-topic for this Zulip

The same thoughts and panic has plagued software engineering but essentially nothing happened of that order has happened.

As stated before accountability is a big reason at play here, Lean is actually a very powerful lever for accountability, as you can just formalize a statement and then let the proof be written by AI and if you trust the Lean Kernel / Checker then you can claim accountability for the proof / correctness.

Furthermore if you believe that mathematicians / software engineers / <INSERT YOUR FAVORITE PROFESSION> can be "automated", then you essentially believe that our society should be run by AI.

Since I initiated this in a way with my first comment on the Knuth thread , allow me to explain a bit more:

  • I believe the effect will be / is a shrinking or downward pressure on the demand for NEWER entrants into math research.
  • AI is a tool , but as many other tools this doesn’t mean it won’t cause labour changes.
  • The Knuth example showed again an expert can use AI in place of a post-doc, yes humans account for it , but it will be a much smaller number of highly sought after experts who have been there for some time.
  • This is happening to software development in many places so not sure why people keep saying it isn’t, even if you feel it’s overblown.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Agreed. Also this discussion is becoming off-topic for this Zulip

For this zulip or channel? Because I note that this zulip has a channel just for maths. It could be there , arguable it could be in this channel, but I have certainly seen topics in maths channel that don’t directly mention Lean before.
No, #maths is supposed to be about maths in the context of lean; this is a lean zulip instance

Kevin Cheung said:

How do you teach the average students these days when they know that AI has far surpassed their abilities?

Isn’t that already the situation in chess? Chess seems still very popular.
People play chess because they want to play chess. Many students take math courses because their programs force them to. Maybe this is the beginning of the end of service teaching.

I think the concern is not that people in general will never do any math for fun, indeed many people even do mental arithmetic for fun even though calculators have existed for a long time. But human calculator as a job did become extinct.

No one is stopping math for fun, however I do think math academia is going to suffer in terms of the amount of people viably able to do it as a career . Indeed this will likely apply to many 'intellectual' jobs that have a large 'training period' , and in which AI ultimately compressed that training period into its model.

Ultimately I agree with the concerns in https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03684 , and the discussion in #Machine Learning for Theorem Proving > Discussion: AI-written mathematical proofs and #general > sloplib strongly overlaps here, in particular I made a comment replying to the mention of chess.

In terms of students, I would refer to that article again, it mentions these concerns well. But teaching will be a more stable part of the job as compared to research, even though both will be affected.

It seems to me that there are two distinct issues : (1) math as a human intellectual activity and (2) math as a prerequisite for another subject. For (1), the example of chess suggests that AI will probably not be a threat. For (2), it seems to me that AI (2a) can greatly improve the education of those students who are interested and (2b) may well threaten many jobs in this field. I think (2a) is all for the good and I don’t know what to do about (2b).

Ching-Tsun Chou said:

It seems to me that there are two distinct issues : (1) math as a human intellectual activity and (2) math as a prerequisite for another subject. For (1), the example of chess suggests that AI will probably not be a threat. For (2), it seems to me that AI (2a) can greatly improve the education of those students who are interested and (2b) may well threaten many jobs in this field. I think (2a) is all for the good and I don’t know what to do about (2b).

You are describing what to me sounds more like a competition issue, as in oversupply of students.

I believe this is already very true in terms of PhD graduates, I think if AI does have a positive impact on people learning math (which I do believe it can) , and this hurts jobs via supply-- thats too bad , but its perhaps the best overall for the growth of math.

The worry I am more concerned with, is the demand side shrinking massively. It is a very tall ask for a student to study so hard without a real job , to surpass both other students, AND the cold utility of the latest reasoning AI. I think that final part is really going to hurt.

That Knuth case , would have been a great task to assign to a PhD student and maybe even a post-Doc to investigate for example. If funds are to be allocated, you may simply need less people it seems. In the long term this may cause an 'ageing' population in mathematicians.

I am also starting to realise it is hard to really describe why this isn't the best overall for the growth of math as opposed to first scenario, but i believe it is certainly not as good of a scenario for the human growth of the mathematical research community.

It is kind of hard to strongly decide on its benefit to progress overall, as you can definitely argue AI will in fact accelerate the rate of progress -- especially initially.

For those arguing against the theme I here, I strongly suggest please read the brilliant article by Jeremy Avigad and honestly reflect on it, especially the conclusion.

Like Avigad I also feel mathematics and mathematicians can have a large positive impact in the age of AI. But this will need honesty and a willingness to adapt.

  • Underestimating AI will not help, especially with relation to typical mathematicians. See the empirical evidence (Avigad and Daniel Litt have superb summaries) and make a judgement.
  • Don't also overestimate mathematicians. It is true that there is no evidence yet that AI can ever come up with breakthroughs like Gromov, Deligne, Shannon etc. But then, most of us cannot either.
  • There is almost a choice between a combination of social-political response + AI denial versus adapting and changing our values drastically. Unfortunately (in my view) the former dominates.
  • As an analogy, the redefining of mathematics is somewhat analogous to battling against synthetic diamonds or insisting on the difference between champagne and sparkling water based on origin.

Since there are ad hominem attacks above let me just say that I am speaking with some experience - I have done mathematics for a couple of decades (in Geometry/Topology but also some Proability, a bit of Math bio) and my grand-advisor is Thurston (I disagree with his heavily quoted essay in the context but his revolutionary mathematics is not in doubt).

Let me quote Demis Hassabis (speaking in Bangalore): If we compare with the history of chess, there was roughly a decade from the late 1990s of Centaur chess, where the best players were human-computer collaborations. We may be similarly entering an age of Centaur science (or will enter it once AI gets a bit stronger). Since science is harder than chess perhaps this phase will be longer - more like 20 years.

To me the above suggests analogies to many of the anti-AI arguments. In some sense suggestions are that instead of becoming parts of centaurs we should do some combination of hobbling horses (since they are bred by evil tech companies) and changing the rules of the race. We can do this in a way by making the trail not flat - but then we get beaten by goats and sheep. So we say that "true sprinting is bipedal" and declare ourselves winners.

Kevin Cheung said:

Our classes here for linear algebra are over 150 students.

I taught a first-year linear algebra course with >700 students, most of whom were engineers. Now my university merged with another similar sized one, and the cohort of first-year engineers is ... massive.

Although I brought up chess in this thread, there is a very important difference between chess and math: chess has a definite and precisely defined goal (namely, checkmate your opponent). There is no such thing in math. It seems to me that math as a human intellectual activity is about human understanding. You literally see the world differently once you understand some mathematics. This doesn’t seem to be something AI by itself can do for you.

Suppose for the sake of argument that tomorrow an AI system comes up with a verified Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that no human can at present understand. Would the mathematical community consider it a very worthwhile activity to try to reformulate the AI proof in a humanly understandable and illuminating way? I’m not a mathematician, but I suspect the answer is yes.

I first learnt the rules of chess in secondary school. Today, I still regularly play chess for fun, by the exact same rules.

I also learnt the rules of integration in secondary school. I'm happy to report that I no longer apply these rules of integration in my day-to-day work! These rules are thoroughly un-fun. I'm happy to let Mathematica (not an LLM!) do integrals for me.

But then I learnt about the Riemann integral. Then I learnt about the Lebesgue integral. I learnt about integrals with respect to a measure. Today I routinely see the integral sign in all sorts of crazy places that 15-year-old me would never in my wildest dreams have ever imagined was even possible. I'm really happy that I'm able to work with some of these integrals (but far from all!) in Lean (not an LLM!).

Wait, I hear you say, what if AI is able to produce the next great revolutionary insight that upends our understanding of integrals?

To that I say, try telling a room full of first-year calculus students about all the wonderful theorems you've proved in "measure theory", and see how many of them care. You can't care about something you don't understand.

By the way, I speak from experience as someone currently being paid to teach those same rules of integration to first-year students. Wait a second, wasn't integration already "solved" by Mathematica years ago? Why am I still being paid to teach integration?

Now you're the first-year student, the AI is telling you about this revolutionary "measure theory", and you're sitting there wondering what measuring things has got anything to do with all these integrals, and why the integral sign is appearing in places it shouldn't be. Oh, maybe it's even trying to tell you these things in Lean. How could you ever tell if this isn't just AI slop?

Maybe, as mathematicians, we are paid for our imagination, and above all, our understanding.
I think chess and math shouldn’t be compared. In chess, we play against opponents but in mathematics we discover truths, try to understand things
I mean a tool that can play better than human is not a problem because we still have opponents to beat
But math is not a competition, it is about discovering truths. If any tool can do that automatically, it would be a big problem
Anyway, I do not think AI can do all what mathematicians do, maybe just many of things that mathematicians do

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

Let me quote Demis Hassabis (speaking in Bangalore): If we compare with the history of chess, there was roughly a decade from the late 1990s of Centaur chess, where the best players were human-computer collaborations. We may be similarly entering an age of Centaur science (or will enter it once AI gets a bit stronger). Since science is harder than chess perhaps this phase will be longer - more like 20 years.

To me the above suggests analogies to many of the anti-AI arguments. In some sense suggestions are that instead of becoming parts of centaurs we should do some combination of hobbling horses (since they are bred by evil tech companies) and changing the rules of the race. We can do this in a way by making the trail not flat - but then we get beaten by goats and sheep. So we say that "true sprinting is bipedal" and declare ourselves winners.

I can't speak for others but I would like to respond to two points:

  1. You compare with mathematics with chess. Chess is a well-defined game with an enumerable set of winning positions, and therefore well-defined. Mathematics is a primarily human endeavour to grasp certain patterns and models in a way that the well-trained minds among us can grasp, reason about, and share with each other. We develop new mathematics as we encounter repeated abstractions after going through several iterations which are important for human understanding and figuring out what works best for us. To think an AI do all this for us falls under the monad tutorial fallacy. It is our struggle to understand things by simplifying them for ourselves that leads us to create new mathematics. Even in a future where AI may be able to resolve any conjecture we state with a formal proof or disproof, it is our innate desire to understand things in simple ways that will decide which theories and conjectures are important or interesting. Without our involvement, AI might come up with its own theories and ideas. It may even try to explain them to us. But I doubt we'd understand or always care for them. Thus mathematics is always a moving target that we humans set and move.

1. Anti-AI arguments fall into several categories. I don't buy into the stochastic parrot nonsense. I believe AI can become a very capable companion in exploring mathematics. However, "we live in a society". And this society operates in ways that are not conducive to sustained intellectual acitvity in the absence of economic interest or incentives. AI dramatically lowers the cost of doing existing mathematics, and current society's response is likely to be to pull back funding from mathematical research. A central question that can tilt the scales in all this is "who owns and controls AI". This is a pertinent question to ask and address. Technology does not exist in isolation from society.

David Michael Roberts said:

I taught a first-year linear algebra course with >700 students, most of whom were engineers. Now my university merged with another similar sized one, and the cohort of first-year engineers is ... massive.

That's really massive. What types of assessments do you give for the class? In-person tests and exams?

Franz Huschenbeth said:

Furthermore if you believe that mathematicians / software engineers / <INSERT YOUR FAVORITE PROFESSION> can be "automated", then you essentially believe that our society should be run by AI.

Why should my belief that something can happen be related to whether I think it should happen?
I believe that the coffee shop barista is a job that can absolutely be automated. (Indeed, my coffee maker at home can do much of what I need.) I still value quite a lot having a human there doing it themselves, and I think it's a job that shouldn't be done by computer/AI/robot.

I feel similar things about how undergrad-level teaching will look in a few years.

@Kevin Cheung Note I said "did". But even still, the course until relatively recently ran by having auto-graded randomly-generated questions using symbolic algebra, biweekly small hand-written assignments marked by tutors on a rotating basis, a mid-semester test that is online and timed, done iirc under supervision, and an in-person paper-based exam.

@Shreyas Srinivas The "mathematics is a fundamentally human activity" argument that you make has become standard and is stated often (as you did) in a declarative fashion.

Let me just say that this is not a law of nature, I don't take this view of mathematics, and at least two (very good) mathematicians also don't like this view (the lower bound two is because they are friends who have said so).

My view has always been (from before the deep learning era) that mathematics is part of natural science, the part where we study things that are fully abstracted.

Let me just say that this is not a law of nature, I don't take this view of mathematics, and at least two (very good) mathematicians also don't like this view (the lower bound two is because they are friends who have said so).

how would you respond to an LLM that says it can predict the position of every planet using data that Johannes Kepler had, but is an inscrutable neural net instead of three simple laws? An AI could be perfectly fine with that. It would have achieved its objective. What use does AI have for abstraction?
What is your point? Your comment has nothing to do with any of the three paras which you quote.
I am making precise statements and fairly limited ones.

Specifically, are you claiming that mathematics is a fundamental human activity is a law of nature? Or that we cannot view mathematics as a natural science (note I am saying can view as a natural science which is not meant to exclude any other views that do not contradict it)? Those are my only two statements.
It’s an illustrative example of why abstraction is not something Ai would need or care about in the same way humans do

Which in turn is meant to suggest that
mathematical abstraction, especially the current stack of abstractions we see, is a distinctly human artefact.

Thus a lot of mathematics that goes into building them would, in my opinion, be human activity, designed by human minds for human minds through struggles that appear distinctive to us: We can’t just run inference on a large neural network in our minds after learning from tomes of data. We need to systematise things. AI has no need to do this (at least not in ways that make sense to us.
One could counter-argue that this need to systematise everything into simple theories is a human limitation that AI can help us overcome.

In case you did not notice, neither of my statements had any mention of AI. I started doing mathematics in the late 1990s and these have been my views since then. Perhaps you are not replying to me and making a separate point (if so I have nothing to say).
Are you making the claim that abstraction is essentially human and there is no meaning (in terms of compression say)? That is a peculiar claim.

Siddhartha Gadgil said:

Are you making the claim that abstraction is essentially human and there is no meaning (in terms of compression say)? That is a peculiar claim.

Yes. That’s my claim. More specifically our current set of abstractions.
And it is in response to your questioning the idea that mathematics is fundamentally a human activity

Shreyas Srinivas said:

the idea that mathematics is fundamentally a human activity

I suggest that further discussion of this topic moves elsewhere
Agreed. But I wish to point out that from that claim it follows that human mathematicians becoming redundant is not a meaningful claim.

Johan Commelin said:

Shreyas Srinivas said:

the idea that mathematics is fundamentally a human activity

I suggest that further discussion of this topic moves elsewhere

Thanks for this.

A different perspective: if by "mathematicians" one means "researchers", as some posts suggest, this group has already been under pressure for several decades (predating AI). Academia produces far more researchers than it can absorb (a trend seen in other disciplines, but perhaps particularly prevalent in "pure" mathematics, even broadly construed). Many mathematicians are already "redundant". AI may further worsen this state of affairs ...
If I were a bit sarcastic, I'd say the main difference now is that many will become annotators for AI systems (cf. #job postings) :face_with_open_eyes_and_hand_over_mouth:
If that creates jobs, is it necessarily a bad thing? But I guess the question is, how many more months will those jobs be available.

Creating poorly paid exploited jobs is not exactly something to be celebrated (thinking of image and video annotators in developing countries right now. There's no way AI companies in my experience are offering professional rates to pay pure mathematicians to help them in jobs like contributing benchmark problems)

I think jobs for mathematicians will not be the problem (assuming willingness to learn / dabble into other domains). A mathematician's skills are valuable in many regards. I personally think mathematicians will play a strong role in being the human bridge between reality and formal systems in various areas, atleast for example software / hardware, in which one can then leverage AI to solve the problems in the formal system.

Another thought experiment to consider is, what if P equals NP? Would human mathematicians be redundant if P = NP?

Well, Kurt Gödel famously speculated about that:
https://www2.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~krajicek/goedel-letter.pdf

Well he formulated the immediate (and obvious) consequence, but did not contemplate, what it would mean for the profession of mathematicians. And while it would make reasoning tasks easier, it would not imply an end to the profession of mathematicians, as reasoning in proofs is not their sole task.

Formulating theories and finding the correct definitions are easy examples to state. I would not be too concerned about "an end" or "redundancy" of mathematicians, even in this world of AI, where AI progress seems to mimic a world, where P = NP.
